#> [1] TRUE
m[]
#> [1] 0.6153846
round(m$data, 2)
#> [1] 0.62
unresolved(m)
#> [1] FALSE

# The value is read from $data; before the result arrives it is an
# "unresolved" NA, and call_mirai() waits for it.
m2 <- mirai({
  Sys.sleep(0.3)
  "late"
})
is.na(m2$data)
#> [1] TRUE
call_mirai(m2)$data
#> [1] "late"

# What is not passed is not there.
m3 <- mirai(overdue_rate(rows, today, days), rows = by_member[[1]],
            today = shelf_today, days = loan_days)
m3[]
#> 'miraiError' chr Error in overdue_rate(rows, today, days): could not find function "overdue_rate"

# An error is a value, not an exception.
m4 <- mirai(stop("boom"))
call_mirai(m4)
is_mirai_error(m4$data)
#> [1] TRUE
is_error_value(m4$data)
#> [1] TRUE
class(m4$data)
#> [1] "miraiError" "errorValue" "try-error"

# A timeout is a value as well: the integer 5.
m5 <- mirai(Sys.sleep(5), .timeout = 200)
call_mirai(m5)$data
#> 'errorValue' int 5 | Timed out
is_error_value(m5$data)
#> [1] TRUE

# mirai_map() maps over a list, one mirai per element, and collects with [].
par <- mirai_map(
  by_member, overdue_rate,
  .args = list(today = shelf_today, days = loan_days)
)[]
identical(par, serial)
#> [1] TRUE

# Extra arguments in ... are objects for the daemons, not arguments of .f.
bad <- mirai_map(1:2, \(x, y) x + y, y = 10)[]
bad[[1]]
#> 'miraiError' chr Error in (function (x, y) : argument "y" is missing, with no default
ok <- mirai_map(1:2, \(x, y) x + y, .args = list(y = 10))[.flat]
ok
#> [1] 11 12

# Errors in a map are returned element by element, so only they can be re-run.
mixed <- mirai_map(list(1, "a", 3), \(x) x + 1)[]
vapply(mixed, is_mirai_error, logical(1))
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE

# Run code on every daemon, for example to load a package.
invisible(everywhere(library(stats)))

# seed makes the random numbers of mirai_map() reproducible, whatever the
# number of daemons.
daemons(0)
daemons(2, seed = 282)
first <- mirai_map(1:4, \(i) rnorm(1))[.flat]
daemons(0)
daemons(3, seed = 282)
second <- mirai_map(1:4, \(i) rnorm(1))[.flat]
daemons(0)
identical(first, second)
#> [1] TRUE

# Without daemons, mirai() starts a fresh background process per request.
m6 <- mirai(Sys.getpid())
call_mirai(m6)$data == Sys.getpid()
#> [1] FALSE
tryCatch(mirai_map(1:2, identity), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "No daemons set.\nUse e.g. `mirai::daemons(6)` to set 6 local daemons."

Source: mirai package documentation: mirai

The remaining arguments of daemons() are for production use. dispatcher = FALSE removes the scheduler (tasks go straight to daemons), memory caps the queued payload, url and remote (built with ssh_config(), cluster_config() for Slurm, SGE, PBS and LSF, http_config() or remote_config()) place daemons on other machines, tls secures the connections, .compute names independent sets of daemons (profiles), and sync = TRUE evaluates tasks in the current process, for debugging. The documentation notes that a package which uses a parallel map should never call daemons() itself, so that the user decides where the work runs; it is the same advice as for plan().

Mirai and the parallel package

mirai also plugs into the parallel API. The mirai documentation says that a miraiCluster is an official cluster type in R 4.5, created with parallel::makeCluster(type = "MIRAI"), which calls mirai::make_cluster(), and that it works with clusterApply(), parLapply(), parLapplyLB() and the other functions of the apply family on a cluster. The first lines of the script at the end of this section use the type with parLapply(). This makes it possible to run code written for the parallel package on mirai daemons, local or remote, without changing it.

purrr::in_parallel and Shiny ExtendedTask

purrr 1.1.0 (2025-07-10) added in_parallel(), a way to make purrr’s map() family parallel with mirai. Its help page: wrap the function passed to .f in in_parallel(), and set mirai::daemons(); without daemons the map falls back to sequential processing, and mirai::require_daemons() makes the lack of daemons an error. in_parallel() also asks for a self-contained function: package functions called with ::, data passed as named arguments in ..., helper functions supplied the same way. It is a thin wrapper around carrier::crate(), and purrr checks that the carrier package (version 0.3.0 or later) is installed: it was not in the test image, so the script shows only that the function exists and the message that the call gives. The fragment below, which was not run, is the shape of its use.

library(purrr)
mirai::daemons(2)

offset <- 10
map_dbl(1:3, in_parallel(\(x) x + offset, offset = offset))

mirai::daemons(0)

Source: purrr package documentation: in_parallel

Shiny has its own use of the same machinery for an app that must not freeze while one user’s long computation runs: the ExtendedTask class, documented in Shiny 1.14.0, wraps a function that returns a promise (a mirai, or a future_promise()) so that the session stays responsive while the task proceeds in the background; each ExtendedTask object accepts one invocation at a time. Shiny reactives themselves run on a single R thread, so one slow reactive blocks every session of the process: that is what promises and ExtendedTask are for. The pages on Shiny apps are in Shiny, plumber and Web APIs; the class is described at Shiny documentation: ExtendedTask.

library(parallel)
library(mirai)

# R 4.6.1 knows a "MIRAI" cluster type: the parallel API on mirai daemons.
cl <- makeCluster(2, type = "MIRAI")
class(cl)
#> [1] "miraiCluster" "cluster"
unlist(parLapply(cl, 1:4, \(i) i^2))
#> [1]  1  4  9 16
stopCluster(cl)

# purrr 1.1.0 added in_parallel(); it needs the carrier package.
exists("in_parallel", asNamespace("purrr"))
#> [1] TRUE
tryCatch(purrr::in_parallel(\(x) x + 1), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "The package \"carrier\" (>= 0.3.0) is required for parallel map."
isTRUE(requireNamespace("carrier", quietly = TRUE))
#> [1] FALSE

# The adapter picks up the daemons you set; without them it runs serially.
exists("ExtendedTask", asNamespace("shiny"))
#> [1] TRUE
daemons(0)

Source: mirai package documentation: Communications Backend for R

Asynchronous without parallel: later, promises and callr

"Asynchronous" and "parallel" are different words, and R needs both. Parallel means several computations progress at the same time on several cores. Asynchronous means that you ask for something, carry on, and are told when the answer arrives; it can be built on one thread. The parallel, future and mirai packages above are asynchronous when you use mcparallel(), future() or mirai() and fetch later. The packages in this section are asynchronous in the second sense, for code that must stay responsive: a Shiny session, a plumber API, an interactive console.

later and promises

The later package (1.4.8) is an event loop for R. later(func, delay) schedules a function to run after a delay in seconds, like JavaScript’s setTimeout; R is single-threaded, so there is no promise that the function runs exactly on time, only that at least the delay has passed. By default scheduled work runs only when no other R code is on the stack, which means when R is sitting at the console prompt; run_now() lets a script, which never reaches the prompt, run the work that is due, and loop_empty() says whether anything is left. The value returned by later() is a function that cancels the callback. The script shows that the function does not run until run_now().

The promises package (1.5.0) represents a value that is not there yet. promise(\(resolve, reject) ...) creates a promise from a function that starts the work and calls resolve(value) or reject(reason) when it finishes; the help page says it is mainly for package authors. You consume it with then(promise, onFulfilled, onRejected), catch() and finally(), which return new promises and so chain with the native pipe: promise |> then(f) |> catch(g). The older promise pipes, %...>% for success and %...!% for errors, are marked superseded in the help page of promises 1.5.0, because the native pipe and the function shorthand made then() and catch() as short. The key point of the script is the order of output: the line after then() prints before the value, because then() only registers what to do and returns. A mirai is a promise through as.promise() (mirai needs the event loop to deliver it, so the script runs the loop until the task has resolved), and future_promise() is a promise-friendly future() that returns a promise and keeps the event loop free. The mirai package has an article on Shiny and plumber (mirai package documentation: Promises (Shiny and Plumber)).

library(later)
library(promises)

# later() schedules a function; nothing runs until the event loop gets
# control. In a script that is run_now(); at the console it is the prompt.
log <- "before"
later(\() log <<- c(log, "ran later"), delay = 0.1)
log
#> [1] "before"
run_now(timeoutSecs = 1)
log
#> [1] "before"    "ran later"

# The value returned by later() cancels the callback.
stop_it <- later(\() cat("never printed\n"), delay = 5)
stop_it()
loop_empty()
#> [1] TRUE

# A promise stands for a value that is not there yet.
slow_value <- promise(\(resolve, reject) {
  later(\() resolve(42), delay = 0.1)
})
class(slow_value)
#> [1] "promise"
slow_value |> then(\(v) cat("got", v, "\n"))
cat("this line comes first\n")
#> this line comes first
while (!loop_empty()) run_now(timeoutSecs = 0.5)
#> got 42

# then() chains, catch() handles a rejection.
failing <- promise(\(resolve, reject) {
  later(\() reject("failed upstream"), delay = 0.1)
})
failing |>
  then(\(v) cat("not reached\n")) |>
  catch(\(e) cat("caught:", conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
while (!loop_empty()) run_now(timeoutSecs = 0.5)
#> caught: failed upstream

# The same with the older promise pipe, which is superseded by then().
slow_value %...>% (\(v) cat("piped", v, "\n"))
while (!loop_empty()) run_now(timeoutSecs = 0.5)
#> piped 42

# A mirai is a promise: as.promise() lets the event loop deliver it.
library(mirai)
daemons(2)
m <- mirai({
  Sys.sleep(0.3)
  "mirai finished"
})
as.promise(m) |> then(\(v) cat(v, "\n"))
while (unresolved(m)) run_now(timeoutSecs = 0.1)
run_now()
daemons(0)

# So is a future, through future_promise() (a promise-friendly future()).
library(future)
plan(multisession, workers = 2)
fp <- future_promise({
  Sys.sleep(0.3)
  "future finished"
})
fp |> then(\(v) cat(v, "\n"))
while (!loop_empty()) run_now(timeoutSecs = 0.5)
#> mirai finished
#> future finished
plan(sequential)

Source: later package documentation: later

callr: a background R process

callr::r_bg(func, args) runs a function in a fresh background R session and returns a process object at once, with is_alive(), wait(), get_result(), get_exit_status(), read_all_output() and kill(); callr::r() is the blocking version. It is the simplest tool for "run this slow script while I keep working", and the way the page on HTTP and Web APIs starts a local server for a test and stops it afterwards. The function runs in a clean session, so what it needs goes in args, and an error in the child is signalled by get_result() as an error of class callr_status_error with the child’s message.

library(callr)

# r_bg() runs a function in a fresh background R process and returns.
bg <- r_bg(function(n) {
  Sys.sleep(0.3)
  sum(seq_len(n))
}, args = list(10L))
class(bg)[1]
#> [1] "r_process"
bg$is_alive()
#> [1] TRUE
invisible(bg$wait())
bg$is_alive()
#> [1] FALSE
bg$get_result()
#> [1] 55
bg$get_exit_status()
#> [1] 0

# The function runs in a clean session: pass what it needs in args.
x <- 1
bad <- r_bg(function() x + 1)
invisible(bad$wait())
tryCatch(bad$get_result(), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "! in callr subprocess.\nCaused by error in `(function () ...`:\n! object 'x' not found"
good <- r_bg(function(x) x + 1, args = list(x = x))
invisible(good$wait())
good$get_result()
#> [1] 2

# Errors in the child are signalled by get_result().
failing <- r_bg(function() stop("child failed"))
invisible(failing$wait())
err <- tryCatch(failing$get_result(), error = identity)
class(err)[1]
#> [1] "callr_status_error"
conditionMessage(err)
#> [1] "! in callr subprocess.\nCaused by error in `(function () ...`:\n! child failed"

# Output can be piped back, and a long job can be killed.
talker <- r_bg(function() {
  cat("hello from the child\n")
  1
}, stdout = "|")
invisible(talker$wait())
talker$read_all_output()
#> [1] "hello from the child\n"

sleeper <- r_bg(function() Sys.sleep(30))
sleeper$is_alive()
#> [1] TRUE
invisible(sleeper$kill())
invisible(sleeper$wait())
sleeper$is_alive()
#> [1] FALSE

# r() is the blocking version.
callr::r(function() Sys.getpid()) == Sys.getpid()
#> [1] FALSE

Source: callr package documentation: r_bg

Threads inside a process: BLAS and data.table

A single R process can use several cores without any of the machinery above, when the compiled code it calls is multi-threaded. Two cases matter, and both interact with the workers you start.

BLAS and LAPACK. R does not implement matrix algebra itself; %*%, crossprod(), solve(), chol(), eigen() and svd() end up in the BLAS and LAPACK libraries, which the Installation and Administration manual says can be replaced by external, usually tuned, libraries (R Installation and Administration: Linear algebra). Several of those, among them OpenBLAS, Intel MKL and Apple’s Accelerate, use multiple threads. The test image has an OpenBLAS build. The manual warns about three consequences: R’s profiling (which uses the SIGPROF signal) may cause problems with a multi-threaded BLAS; a multi-threaded BLAS can take more CPU time, and even more elapsed time, than a single-threaded one, especially on a machine running other tasks; and BLAS calls inside threaded code, such as OpenMP sections in packages like mgcv, may be unsafe with some external libraries. The number of threads is set by environment variables read when the library is loaded: OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS or OMP_NUM_THREADS for OpenBLAS (depending on the build, as the manual explains for the Fedora packages), and MKL_NUM_THREADS or OMP_NUM_THREADS for MKL (R Installation and Administration: OpenBLAS and BLIS). Changing the variable inside a running session is too late for the library. The RhpcBLASctl package (not installed in the test image, so not run) exists to change the BLAS thread count at run time, with functions such as blas_set_num_threads() and omp_set_num_threads(); setting the variable before the worker starts, as below, needs no package.

data.table. data.table (1.18.6.1) parallelises fread(), fwrite(), grouping, ordering and other operations with OpenMP. Its help page for setDTthreads() says the number of threads is initialised when data.table is loaded, from environment variables, to 50% of the logical CPUs by default; getDTthreads() reports it; setDTthreads(threads) changes it for the session (0 means all logical CPUs); setDTthreads(NULL) reads the environment variables again; and the variables R_DATATABLE_NUM_THREADS (a fixed number), R_DATATABLE_NUM_PROCS_PERCENT and OMP_THREAD_LIMIT (which caps everything) control the initial value. The help page also says that data.table automatically switches to single-threaded mode in a fork, as the one made by mclapply() (and by the foreach package), because nested parallelism would overload the CPUs, and that by default it is multi-threaded again afterwards (restore_after_fork). A PSOCK worker is not a fork, it loads data.table fresh and gets the full default, which is why two workers can oversubscribe a machine.

How many cores a job keeps busy can be measured without timing anything: it is the CPU time (user plus system) divided by the elapsed time. The first part of the script does that in three fresh R processes started with callr, which can be given a different environment: with the default environment the matrix products keep more than two cores busy; with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 they keep one; with 2 they keep two. The ratios are rounded, and the first only compared with 2, because it depends on the machine and the BLAS. The rest shows data.table: the thread count in the master, in two forked children (one thread each), and in two PSOCK workers that were started after the environment variables had been set (also one: the variables are read when each worker loads data.table). The master loaded data.table before the variables were set, so it needed setDTthreads(threads = NULL) to read them. The usual rule of thumb is that workers multiplied by threads per worker should not exceed the cores available: with n workers, give each cores / n threads, or one.

library(parallel)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))

# Threads inside one R process: a multi-threaded BLAS is one example. How
# many cores a job keeps busy is CPU time divided by elapsed time.
busy <- function() {
  set.seed(1)
  m <- matrix(rnorm(1500 * 1500), 1500)
  t <- system.time(for (i in 1:3) crossprod(m))
  unname((t[["user.self"]] + t[["sys.self"]]) / t[["elapsed"]])
}
# A fresh R process for each measurement, with the BLAS thread count set in
# its environment before it starts. The numbers depend on the machine and
# its BLAS; the shape does not.
default <- callr::r(busy)
one <- callr::r(
  busy, env = c(callr::rcmd_safe_env(), OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS = "1")
)
two <- callr::r(
  busy, env = c(callr::rcmd_safe_env(), OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS = "2")
)
default > 2
#> [1] TRUE
round(one)
#> [1] 1
round(two)
#> [1] 2

# data.table is multi-threaded too (OpenMP), with its own controls.
getDTthreads() >= 2L
#> [1] TRUE

# Inside a forked child it drops to one thread, to avoid nested parallelism.
unlist(mclapply(1:2, \(i) getDTthreads(), mc.cores = 2))
#> [1] 1 1

# A PSOCK worker is a new session: it starts with the full thread count, so
# two workers can oversubscribe the machine. Limit it before it starts.
Sys.setenv(
  R_DATATABLE_NUM_THREADS = "1",
  OMP_NUM_THREADS = "1",
  OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS = "1"
)
cl <- makeCluster(2)
unlist(clusterEvalQ(cl, Sys.getenv("OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS")))
#> [1] "1" "1"
unlist(clusterEvalQ(cl, {
  library(data.table)
  getDTthreads()
}))
#> [1] 1 1
stopCluster(cl)

# data.table reads its environment variable when it is loaded, so this
# session needs setDTthreads() to read it again.
getDTthreads() >= 2L
#> [1] TRUE
invisible(setDTthreads(threads = NULL))
getDTthreads()
#> [1] 1

Source: data.table package documentation: setDTthreads and getDTthreads

Choosing a tool

The five ways to parallelise overdue_rate() over the members all return exactly the same list. That is what to check first when moving a computation to workers: the parallel result must be identical to the serial one, apart from random numbers. The script runs the four that were not compared earlier together (forked, PSOCK, future.apply and mirai) and checks each with identical() against the serial result.

source("scenario.R")
library(parallel)
library(future)
library(future.apply)
library(mirai)

overdue_rate <- function(rows, today, days) {
  end <- rows$return_date
  end[is.na(end)] <- today
  mean(as.integer(end - rows$loan_date) > days, na.rm = TRUE)
}
members <- tolower(trimws(loans$member))
keep <- nzchar(members)
by_member <- split(loans[keep, ], members[keep])
serial <- lapply(by_member, overdue_rate, today = shelf_today, days = loan_days)

forked <- mclapply(
  by_member, overdue_rate,
  today = shelf_today, days = loan_days, mc.cores = 2
)

cl <- makeCluster(2)
socket <- parLapply(
  cl, by_member, overdue_rate, today = shelf_today, days = loan_days
)
stopCluster(cl)

plan(multisession, workers = 2)
futures <- future_lapply(
  by_member, overdue_rate, today = shelf_today, days = loan_days
)
plan(sequential)

daemons(2)
mirais <- mirai_map(
  by_member, overdue_rate,
  .args = list(today = shelf_today, days = loan_days)
)[]
daemons(0)

results <- list(
  fork = forked, psock = socket, future = futures, mirai = mirais
)
vapply(results, identical, logical(1), y = serial)
#>   fork  psock future  mirai
#>   TRUE   TRUE   TRUE   TRUE

Source: R documentation: identical

The table summarises where each tool fits.

Tool Works on Starts workers by Use it when

mclapply(), pvec(), mcparallel()

Linux and macOS (Windows runs serially)

forking

a quick speed-up on one Unix machine, outside RStudio and GUIs, with no multi-threaded library in the way

makeCluster() with parLapply() and friends

everywhere

Rscript over sockets (PSOCK), or forking

you want base R only, one pool for many calls, workers on other machines, and full control of what is exported

future with future.apply (or furrr)

everywhere, forking where allowed

chosen by plan()

code that must run unchanged on a laptop, on a server and on a scheduler; reproducible random numbers with future.seed; automatic globals

mirai with mirai_map()

everywhere

persistent daemons, local or remote

low-latency tasks, many small jobs, error values instead of exceptions, remote daemons, Shiny and plumber; parallel and purrr adapters

callr::r_bg()

everywhere

a fresh background R process

one long job you want to leave running, a test server, a process you must be able to kill

later and promises

everywhere

no new process: an event loop

code that waits for something (a task, a timer, a request) and must stay responsive

Source: R documentation: mclapply

Pitfalls at a glance

  • Parallelising before measuring. Find the slow part first (Performance, Profiling and Benchmarking); a vectorised or compiled version of the same step is often faster than any number of workers.

  • Tasks that are too small. Dispatch and serialisation cost more than the work. Make fewer, larger chunks (chunk.size, future.chunk.size, a function that handles a whole group).

  • Globals. A worker has none of your variables. Pass them as arguments, export them once with clusterExport(), or use a framework that finds them (future) or asks for them by name (mirai).

  • Random numbers. Use L’Ecuyer-CMRG streams, one per task if the result must not depend on the number of workers; never set.seed(i) in each worker.

  • Too many workers. More workers than cores, or workers times threads above the cores, makes everything slower. Use parallelly::availableCores(), leave a core free, and limit BLAS and data.table threads in the workers.

  • Forking where it is unsafe. In RStudio and other GUIs, with graphics devices open, and with multi-threaded libraries; use a PSOCK cluster or plan(multisession).

  • Forgotten clusters and plans. on.exit(stopCluster(cl)), plan(sequential) at the end of a script, daemons(0) when done.

  • Order and errors. The results come back in the order of the input, but a worker’s error is reported once, with a useless call; reproduce a failure with lapply() on a small input.

  • Large results. Everything returned is serialised through a pipe or a socket; reduce on the worker and return the summary.

Version notes

The entries come from the NEWS files of R (R NEWS; the entries before R 4.0.0 are in R NEWS: Changes in R 3.x), the parallel vignette and the NEWS pages of the packages.

Version Change

R 2.14.0

The parallel package is first included, merging the multicore (forking) and snow (sockets) packages and adding integrated random-number handling. R 2.14.1 fixed tempfile() choosing the same name in two processes.

R 3.3.0

detectCores() has logical = TRUE as the default on all platforms; only Sparc Solaris was affected.

R 3.4.0

The low-level functions that pass serialised objects to and from forked children support long vectors on 64-bit platforms. Loading the parallel namespace no longer sets or changes .Random.seed, even if R_PARALLEL_PORT is unset.

R 3.5.0

getDefaultCluster() is added to get the cluster set by setDefaultCluster(). mclapply(), pvec() and mcparallel() (with mccollect()) no longer leave zombie processes. The default number of chunks of parLapplyLB() and parSapplyLB() becomes twice the number of nodes.

R 3.5.2

Fork clusters could hang because of a race condition in the initialisation of makeCluster(); fixed.

R 3.6.0

The default method of generating from a discrete uniform distribution, used by sample(), changes (sample.kind = "Rejection"); RNGkind() also returns the kind used by sample(). On Windows detectCores() detects processors in all processor groups, and clusterApplyLB() no longer hangs with more than 64 workers.

R 4.0.0

Starting a homogeneous PSOCK cluster on localhost with many nodes is much faster. mcmapply() preserves the attributes of "try-error" results and never simplifies them.

R 4.0.1

mclapply(..., mc.preschedule = FALSE) handles raw vector results correctly. detectCores(all.tests = TRUE) tries the matching operating system first.

R 4.1.0

mclapply() and pvec() no longer terminate processes started earlier by mcparallel() and related calls. detectCores() drops support for IRIX.

R 4.1.2

Selecting the Marsaglia-Multicarry generator warns in more places.

R 4.2.0

sample() and sample.int() have additional sanity checks on their size and n arguments.

R 4.5.0

The mirai documentation names makeCluster(type = "MIRAI") as an official cluster type in R 4.5. The R NEWS does not mention registerClusterType() or the types, so no exact version is given for them.

R 4.6.1

The parallel package is version 4.6.1; the help page of makeCluster() lists the types "PSOCK", "FORK", "MIRAI", "MPI", "RPSOCK" and "SOCK". No other parallel-related entry was found in the R 4.x NEWS than those above.

future 1.20.0

availableCores(), availableWorkers(), makeClusterPSOCK() and supportsMulticore() start to move to the parallelly package; plan(multiprocess) is deprecated.

future 1.32.0, 1.33.0

multiprocess becomes defunct (1.32.0, 2023-03-07) and is removed (1.33.0, 2023-07-01).

future 1.40.0

with(plan(...), expr) and local = TRUE evaluate under a temporary plan (2025-04-10).

future 1.67.0

plan(multisession) defaults to availableCores(constraints = "connections-16") (2025-07-29).

purrr 1.1.0

in_parallel() is added for parallel maps powered by mirai (2025-07-10); purrr 1.2.0 lets it accept helper functions supplied in ....

promises 1.5.0

The promise pipes (%...>% and the others) are superseded by then(), catch() and finally() with the native pipe.

Source: R NEWS: Changes in R 4.0.0 to 4.6.1

Where older tutorials differ

Older tutorial writes Current practice Why Since

library(snow) or library(multicore)

library(parallel)

the two packages were merged into parallel, with integrated random-number handling

R 2.14.0

doParallel and registerDoParallel(cores = detectCores()) with foreach(...) %dopar%

parLapply(), future_lapply() or mirai_map(); keep foreach only for existing code (doParallel and foreach were not installed here, so nothing about them was run)

%dopar% hides the backend, the exports and the random numbers behind a registered global, and the same loop silently runs serially when no backend is registered

always

doMC and registerDoMC()

a PSOCK cluster, or plan(multisession)

doMC is forking only, so it fails on Windows and in RStudio

always

set.seed(i) in each worker

clusterSetRNGStream(), mc.set.seed with L’Ecuyer-CMRG, future.seed, daemons(seed =)

different seeds do not guarantee independent streams

always

cl <- makeCluster(detectCores())

makeCluster(max(1L, parallelly::availableCores() - 1L))

detectCores() may be NA, ignores container and scheduler limits, and leaves no core for the master

always

parSapply(cl, ...)

vapply(parLapply(cl, ...), ..., numeric(1))

sapply()-style simplification makes the type of the result depend on the data

always

mclapply() in a script that must run on Windows or in RStudio

a socket cluster or plan(multisession); forking only where parallelly::supportsMulticore() says so

forking is not available on Windows and discouraged in GUIs by the help pages

always

a cluster started and never stopped

on.exit(stopCluster(cl)) in the function that made it

idle workers keep their sockets and memory until the session ends

always

plan(multiprocess)

plan(multisession) or plan(multicore)

removed from future

future 1.33.0

future::availableCores()

parallelly::availableCores()

the function moved to parallelly

future 1.20.0

promise %...>% f()

promise |> then(f)

the promise pipes are superseded

promises 1.5.0

purrr::map(x, ~ f(.x)) run with a hand-made cluster

purrr::map(x, in_parallel(function(x) f(x))) with mirai::daemons()

purrr runs the map on mirai daemons itself

purrr 1.1.0

Source: R documentation: mclapply

Where to go next

  • Performance, Profiling and Benchmarking to find what is worth parallelising and to measure whether it was.

  • Memory and Copy Semantics for the copy-on-modify that makes a forked child cheap, and what a worker costs in memory.

  • Distributions and Random Numbers for the generators, set.seed() and sample(), and the simulations (replicate()) that are the usual parallel workload.

  • Interfacing C, C++ and Fortran for moving the hot loop to compiled code, including OpenMP, instead of adding workers.

  • The apply Family and Functionals and Vectorisation and Iteration for the serial versions of everything above.

  • data.table for its internal threading, setDTthreads() and the operations it parallelises.

  • Matrices and Arrays for the BLAS and LAPACK libraries behind multi-threaded matrix algebra.

  • HTTP and Web APIs and Shiny, plumber and Web APIs for background processes and non-blocking apps.

  • Conditions and Error Handling for tryCatch() and withCallingHandlers(), used throughout this page.

  • Concurrency and Async in Python for the same ideas (processes, threads, event loops) in another language, and Python Reference.
